steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Diabetes Type 1 focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Diabetes Type 1.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Diabetes Type 1 require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Diabetes Type 1.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, levocetirizine) require 50% dose reduction in renal impairment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Fexofenadine undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism; preferred in hepatic impairment.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Cetirizine, loratadine, and budesonide nasal spray have strong safety track records in pregnancy.
special_populations.elderly: First-generation antihistamines are Beers criteria listed; cause severe urinary retention and fall risk.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is type 1 diabetes? Diabetes means your blood glucose , also called blood sugar, is too high. With type 1 diabetes, your body makes little or no insulin. Insulin is a hormone from your pancreas that helps glucose move from your body into your cells, where it is used for energy. Your body can make glucose, but it also comes from the food you eat. Without insulin, too much glucose stays in your blood. Over time, high blood glucose can lead to serious problems with your heart , eyes , kidneys , nerves , gums, and teeth. If your blood glucose gets very high, you can develop diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). It happens when your body doesn't have enough insulin to allow glucose into your cells. Instead, your liver breaks down fat for energy, which produces ketones. When ketones build up too quickly, they can reach dangerous levels. DKA is a life-threatening emergency. What causes type 1 diabetes? Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease . Your immune system mistakenly attacks the cells in your pancreas that make insulin. Researchers don't yet know exactly why this happens. Genes and environmental factors may play a role in triggering the disease. Who is more likely to develop type 1 diabetes? Type 1 diabetes often begins in children and young adults, but it can appear at any age. Having a parent or sibling with type 1 diabetes may increase your chance of developing it. What are the symptoms of type 1 diabetes? Symptoms often start quickly, especially in children. In adults, they may develop more slowly. Symptoms may include: Feeling very thirsty Feeling very hungry Urinating (peeing) more often, including at night Having fatigue Having blurry vision Losing feeling in your feet, or having tingling in your feet or hands Having sores that don't heal Losing weight without trying How is type 1 diabetes diagnosed? Blood tests that measure your blood glucose level can show whether it is higher than normal for you. What are the treatments for type 1 diabetes? Type 1 diabetes is a chronic (long-term) condition. You will need daily insulin, either through injections or an insulin pump. Some people also take another diabetes medicine that works with insulin. Ask your health care provider about the best way to check your blood glucose level and how often you should check it. Can type 1 diabetes be prevented? Type 1 diabetes can't be prevented. But you may be able to prevent or delay health problems related to diabetes by: Managing your blood glucose level with finger prick tests or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) Making healthy food choices Getting regular exercise A blood test called the A1C can show how well you are managing your diabetes over time. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
